summary: An experimental document describing how multicast can be supported efficiently among routers inside one ATM logical IP subnet using Sparse Mode PIM, without needing a Multicast Address Resolution Server.

eli5.summary: A way for routers on one special network to send the same message to a whole group at once, without using a middleman.

subtitle: Multicast routing over ATM without needing a dedicated server.

tldr.problem: Supporting IP multicast among routers in a single ATM logical IP subnet requires the Multicast Address Resolution Server (MARS), which is complex and adds overhead.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC shows how PIM-SM routers connected to ATM can use explicit join messages to automatically create point-to-multipoint virtual circuits (VCs) for multicast groups, bypassing the need for a separate MARS server.
tldr.outcome: The method simplifies intra-LIS multicast between routers by taking advantage of PIM-SM's join mechanism, reducing complexity compared to MARS at the cost of being specific to PIM-SM and router-to-router multicast.

facts.label: Shared VC per router
facts.value: One, to all other routers in LIS

today: RFC 2337 is an Experimental protocol. It provides a simpler alternative to MARS for PIM-SM routers in a single ATM subnet, though MARS remains the more general solution.

sections.title: Multicast Routing on ATM Networks
sections.content:
ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) is a networking technology that supports point-to-multipoint virtual circuits (VCs)—paths where one source can send data to multiple destinations in one operation. IP multicast, defined in the IP protocol, also delivers one message to many recipients. Combining them efficiently is not straightforward. RFC 2022 defined MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server), a separate server that maps IP multicast groups to ATM VCs. However, MARS adds complexity and overhead.

This RFC describes a simpler approach for a specific case: when all the routers are in a single Logical IP Subnet (LIS)—that is, they all share the same ATM network segment—and when they all run PIM-SM (Protocol Independent Multicast Sparse Mode). PIM-SM routers already exchange join messages to tell each other they want to receive a multicast group. This RFC exploits that mechanism: instead of a separate MARS server, the routers use the join messages themselves to trigger the creation of the right VCs.
sections.eli5: On a special network type called ATM, routers can send one message to many others. Instead of using a middleman server to organize it, the routers can just tell each other directly.

sections.title: How Routers Build the Network
sections.content:
Each PIM-SM router in a LIS must know the IP and ATM addresses of all other routers in that LIS. This knowledge can come from an ARP (Address Resolution) server or from static configuration. Every router maintains a single shared point-to-multipoint VC rooted at that router, with all other routers in the LIS as leaf nodes. This shared VC is used to forward multicast control messages (PIM join/prune messages) and data packets to all multicast groups.

In addition, a router can create dedicated, group-specific point-to-multipoint VCs. When an upstream router for a multicast group receives a PIM join message from a downstream router, it can add that downstream router as a leaf on a dedicated VC for that group. When a downstream router sends a prune message (saying it no longer wants the group), the upstream router removes it from the VC. This way, traffic is more efficiently routed: a multicast group uses a dedicated VC only to the routers that need it, rather than sending everything to all routers.
sections.eli5: Each router has one path to all other routers for sending control messages, and then creates separate paths for each group to save bandwidth.

sections.title: Switching to Source Trees
sections.content:
In PIM-SM, routers can use a shared tree rooted at a Rendezvous Point (RP) for a multicast group, or they can switch to a source-rooted tree for a specific source. The RFC requires that when one router in a LIS switches to a source tree (by sending (S,G) PIM joins), all other routers in the LIS that have downstream members for that group must also switch. Since these switch messages are sent over the shared VC, other routers can detect the switch and follow suit.

A special case is when a new router joins after the switch: the new router must detect that it has been added to a source-rooted VC by observing (S,G) traffic arriving on a VC it did not explicitly join. Upon detecting this, the router should send its own (S,G) joins to the source so it properly switches to the source tree.

The RFC also notes a potential issue when a router receives a multicast packet from another router in its own LIS: it must not send the packet back on any of the LIS distribution VCs, to avoid "packet reflection."
sections.eli5: When one router learns about a direct path to the source, the others figure it out from the traffic they see.

sections.title: Security and MARS Comparison
sections.content:
The security considerations are inherited from PIM-SM itself. The RFC notes that multicast routing protocols historically lack strong authentication, and several threats exist: unauthorized senders, unauthorized receivers, unauthorized use of the Rendezvous Point, and unauthorized switching to shortest-path trees. Strong cryptographic authentication (such as Keyed HMAC-MD5) could be added to the routing protocol, or the IP Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Payload protocols could be used to protect multicast routing messages.

Compared to MARS, this approach is simpler and requires no new encapsulation—it works with standard LLC/SNAP or NLPID encapsulation. It avoids the cost and complexity of MARS. The trade-off is that the method is specific to PIM-SM and handles only router-to-router multicast within a single LIS, whereas MARS is more general and supports host participation and multiple LISs.
sections.eli5: Keeping multicast safe requires protecting the control messages from tampering, the same way you protect other network messages.
